title: Formal and Informal Register
bigQuestion: How do you know when Spanish calls for usted and Atentamente, and when it calls for tú and un abrazo?

story.title: Two Letters for One Job
story.kicker: A senior writes to a Pilsen company for a summer job, and his first draft sounds like a text to a friend.
paragraphs: Andrés is a senior at a high school in Chicago's Back of the Yards. In April he sees a flyer in a bakery window on 18th Street: a family-owned catering company is hiring summer help, and the owner wants applications in Spanish, because the kitchen and most of the clients speak it. Andrés speaks Spanish every day with his grandmother and his friends. He sits down that night and types his first draft in ten minutes.

"Hola! Vi el anuncio y quiero trabajar con ustedes este verano. Soy buena onda y trabajo duro. Me puedes llamar cuando quieras. Gracias!! Andrés." (Hi! I saw the ad and I want to work with you this summer. I am cool and I work hard. You can call me whenever. Thanks!! Andrés.) He reads it over. Every word is Spanish. Every word is correct. Something is still wrong, and he cannot say what.

He shows it to his aunt Rocío, who works in an office in the Loop. She reads it and laughs, kindly. "Andrés, así le escribes a tu primo. Esta señora no te conoce." (Andrés, that is how you write to your cousin. This lady does not know you.) She points at *me puedes llamar*. "Tú. Le hablas de tú a la dueña de una empresa." (Tú. You are addressing the owner of a company as tú.) Then at *buena onda*. "Eso es para tus amigos." (That is for your friends.)

Together they write a second letter. "Estimada señora Herrera: Le escribo para solicitar el puesto de ayudante de cocina que anunció en su tienda. Soy estudiante de último año, hablo inglés y español, y tengo experiencia sirviendo en eventos de mi parroquia. Estoy disponible de junio a agosto. Le agradezco su atención y quedo a su disposición. Atentamente, Andrés Maldonado." (Dear Mrs. Herrera: I am writing to apply for the kitchen assistant position you posted in your shop. I am a senior, I speak English and Spanish, and I have experience serving at events at my parish. I am available from June to August. Thank you for your attention; I remain at your disposal. Sincerely, Andrés Maldonado.)

The two letters say almost the same thing. The difference is *el registro* (register): the level of formality a situation calls for, carried by the pronoun, the verb endings, the greetings and the word choices. Andrés already had two registers in his mouth; he used one with his grandmother's friends and another with his teammates. He had just never written the formal one down. This chapter is about learning to hear that difference and choose on purpose, in speech, in letters, in messages, and in the signs, menus and headlines you read every day.
story.think: Think of a message you would send to a friend and one you would send to a school principal about the same thing. What would you change besides the words?

lessons.title: Tú, Usted and Vos
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish has more than one word for you; tú and vos are for people you are close to, and usted is for people you show respect or distance to.
reading: Andrés's first mistake was one word: *me puedes llamar* instead of *me puede llamar*. That word is you. English has one you for everyone. Spanish has *tú*, *usted* and, in some countries, *vos*, and choosing among them is the first act of register. Tú (and vos where it is used) is for friends, family, classmates, children and anyone your own age in a casual setting. *Usted* is for adults you do not know, elders, teachers, bosses, customers, officials, and anyone you want to show respect.

Usted uses the same verb forms as él and ella. "¿Cómo está usted?" (How are you?) uses está, not estás. "¿Puede llamarme?" (Can you call me?) uses puede, not puedes. The possessive is *su* ("su tienda," your shop) and the object pronoun is *le* or *lo/la*. In writing, usted is often abbreviated *Ud.* or *Vd.* Because usted forms look like third-person forms, a sentence like "¿Tiene tiempo?" can mean Do you have time? or Does he have time? Context, and sometimes adding usted, makes it clear.

The choice is not the same everywhere. In Spain, tú is used very widely, even with strangers in shops and with many teachers. In Mexico, usted is more common with elders and in business. In Colombia and Costa Rica, many families use usted even with parents and children, as a form of affection. In Argentina, vos does the job of tú. When in doubt, start with usted. Being too formal is a small awkwardness; being too familiar can feel disrespectful.

Notice what happened with Andrés. His grammar was right for tú. The problem was that the reader was a business owner he had never met. Register is not about correct forms. It is about the right forms for the person in front of you. The verb *tutear* means to address someone as tú, and *tratar de usted* means to address someone as usted. Both are things you do on purpose.

words.d: register — the level of formality of speech or writing, set by pronoun, verb, greeting and word choice
you (formal) — uses the él/ella verb forms: ¿Cómo está usted?; abbreviated Ud.
you (informal) — for friends, family and peers: ¿Cómo estás?
to address someone as tú — Puedes tutearme means You can call me tú
to address someone as usted — Trato de usted a mis maestros (I address my teachers as usted)

look.title: One Question, Two Registers
look.text: To a classmate: ¿Tienes un minuto? ¿Me puedes ayudar con la tarea? (Do you have a minute? Can you help me with the homework?) To a teacher: ¿Tiene usted un minuto? ¿Me puede ayudar con la tarea? Same question, same words except the verb endings and the pronoun. To the owner of a company: Señora Herrera, ¿tiene usted un minuto? Quisiera hablar con usted sobre el puesto. (Mrs. Herrera, do you have a minute? I would like to speak with you about the position.)
look.prompt: Which verbs change between the first and second versions? What does the third version add that the second does not?

check.q: Which sentence correctly addresses a school principal you have just met?
check.why: Usted takes the él/ella form: está. Estás is the tú form and cannot go with usted; estáis is vosotros.

check.q: In which country do many families use usted with parents and children as a sign of affection?
check.why: In Colombia and Costa Rica, usted is common inside families. Spain uses tú very widely, and Argentina uses vos.

check.q: "Puedes tutearme" means
choices: You can address me as usted.
You can address me as tú.
check.why: Tutear means to use tú with someone. Puedes tutearme is an invitation to drop usted.

lessons.title: Titles and Names
lessons.mainIdea: Señor, señora, don and doña, and professional titles like licenciado and doctora go with usted, and they are written in lowercase except when abbreviated.
reading: Rocío's first change to Andrés's letter was the greeting: "Estimada señora Herrera." A title with a last name is the natural partner of usted. *Señor* (Mr.) and *señora* (Mrs., Ms.) go with a last name: el señor Herrera, la señora Herrera. *Señorita* (Miss) was once common for unmarried women; today many people prefer señora for any adult woman, and señorita is heard less. When you speak directly to someone, the article drops: "Buenos días, señora Herrera."

*Don* and *doña* are titles of respect that go with a first name, not a last name: don Manuel, doña Carmen. They are used for elders and respected people in a community, and you hear them constantly in Mexican, Central American and Caribbean neighborhoods: "Buenas tardes, doña Rosa." You would never say don Herrera. Professional titles are also common. *Licenciado* or *licenciada* (someone with a university degree, very common in Mexico), *doctor* or *doctora*, *profesor* or *profesora*, *ingeniero* or *ingeniera*, and *maestro* or *maestra* (teacher) all take usted.

Capitalization trips up English speakers. In Spanish, titles are lowercase when written out: señor García, doña Carmen, el doctor Ruiz. They are capitalized only in their abbreviations: Sr. García, Sra. Herrera, Dr. Ruiz, Dra. Soto, Lic. Torres, Prof. Vega, D. Manuel, Dña. Carmen. So a letter opens "Estimado Sr. García:" or "Estimado señor García:" and both are correct.

One more detail: a Spanish letter greeting ends with a colon, not a comma. "Estimada señora Herrera:" then a new line. In English you would write "Dear Mrs. Herrera,". Small marks like this tell a reader that you know the conventions, and that is a large part of what register does.

words.d: Mr., sir — with a last name: el señor Herrera; abbreviated Sr.
Mrs., Ms., ma'am — with a last name: la señora Herrera; abbreviated Sra.
a title of respect with a first name: don Manuel, doña Carmen; abbreviated D. and Dña.
a person with a university degree, used as a title in Mexico: el licenciado Torres, Lic. Torres
the title — señor, doctora and licenciado are títulos; lowercase unless abbreviated

look.title: Who Gets Which Title?
look.text: Andrés walks into the bakery. Behind the counter is the owner, Carmen Herrera, about sixty. Next to her is her son, Luis, about thirty, who runs the catering side and has a business degree. A regular customer, an older man everyone calls Manuel, is drinking coffee. Andrés says: "Buenos días, señora Herrera. Buenos días, licenciado." Luis smiles: "Dime Luis, y puedes tutearme." The owner nods toward the customer: "Y él es don Manuel."
look.prompt: Why does Andrés use señora with one person and licenciado with another? What does don Manuel tell you about how the community sees the customer?

check.q: Which is written correctly?
check.why: Señor is lowercase when spelled out, the last name is capitalized, and a Spanish letter greeting ends with a colon. Don goes with a first name, not a last name.

check.q: Which title goes with a first name?
check.why: Don and doña take a first name: doña Carmen. Señor, señora and licenciado take a last name.

check.q: "Buenas tardes, doctora Soto. ¿Cómo está?" What register is this, and why?
choices: Informal, because it uses a first name
Formal, because it uses a title and the usted form está
Informal, because buenas tardes is casual
Formal, because it uses the tú form está
check.why: A professional title with a last name and the usted verb form está mark the sentence as formal. Está is the usted form, not the tú form (estás).

lessons.title: Switching Register Mid-Conversation
lessons.mainIdea: When someone says puedes tutearme, every usted form in your speech shifts to tú: está becomes estás, su becomes tu, le becomes te.
reading: Luis told Andrés, "Puedes tutearme." What happens next is a real skill: switching from usted to tú without dropping a form. Everything connected to you changes together. The verb: "¿Cómo está?" becomes "¿Cómo estás?" The possessive: "su empresa" (your company) becomes "tu empresa." The object pronoun: "Le agradezco" (I thank you) becomes "Te agradezco." Commands: "Dígame" (tell me) becomes "Dime." Even the reflexive: "Siéntese" (sit down) becomes "Siéntate."

The reverse switch, from tú up to usted, is just as important and happens more often than you think. A friend introduces you to her grandmother. Your classmate's father answers the phone. A teacher you joke with in the hall is interviewing you for a scholarship. In each case, the tú you were using needs to become usted, and all the pieces move with it: tienes → tiene, tu → su, te → le, habla → hable, ven → venga.

There are signals that tell you which register a speaker wants. If an adult addresses you as tú and invites you to do the same, you may. If an adult addresses you as tú but keeps a title and formal tone, that is normal; adults often say tú to young people while expecting usted back. That is not rude. It reflects age and role, and it is how Andrés's grandmother's friends speak to him. Answering them with usted is a sign that he was raised well, and in many families that matters a great deal.

The safest habit: begin with usted for any adult you do not know well, listen for "tutéame" or "puedes tutearme" or "háblame de tú," and switch fully when invited. If you slip and say tú by mistake, a quick "perdón, usted" fixes it. Native speakers correct themselves this way all the time.

words.d: closeness, trust — tener confianza con alguien means to be on close enough terms to use tú
respect — usted, titles and formal greetings are ways of showing respeto
the boss — la jefa for a woman; usually addressed as usted until told otherwise
speak to me as tú — an invitation to switch to the informal register
sorry, excuse me — a quick way to correct a slip: Perdón, usted

look.title: Every Piece Moves Together
look.text: Formal: Señora Herrera, ¿tiene usted un momento? Quisiera mostrarle mi horario. Si le parece bien, puedo empezar en junio. Dígame qué día le conviene. (Mrs. Herrera, do you have a moment? I would like to show you my schedule. If it seems fine to you, I can start in June. Tell me which day suits you.) Informal, to Luis: Luis, ¿tienes un momento? Quisiera mostrarte mi horario. Si te parece bien, puedo empezar en junio. Dime qué día te conviene.
look.prompt: Underline every word that changed between the two versions. How many are there? Which ones are verbs and which are pronouns?

check.q: A boss says "Puedes tutearme." Which sentence correctly follows that invitation?
check.why: After the invitation, the verb shifts to the tú form tienes. Tiene with tu mixes usted and tú; tenéis is the vosotros form.

check.q: Which sentence correctly shifts "Te agradezco tu ayuda" to the usted register?
check.why: Both the object pronoun and the possessive must shift: te → le and tu → su. Mixing one of each is a common error.

check.q: An adult you just met addresses you as tú but keeps a formal tone. What should you do?
choices: Answer with tú, since they started it
Correct them and ask for usted
Answer with usted unless they invite you to switch
Stop speaking Spanish and use English
check.why: Adults often say tú to young people while expecting usted back. Keep usted until you hear puedes tutearme or a similar invitation.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Formal Letter
lessons.mainIdea: A formal Spanish letter opens with Estimado or Estimada plus a title and a colon, states its purpose in the first sentence, and closes with Atentamente.
reading: Rocío and Andrés's second letter follows a shape that Spanish speakers use for job applications, complaints, requests to a school, and business email. At the top, the place and date: "Chicago, 14 de abril de 2026." Notice the pattern: city, comma, day, de, month in lowercase, de, year. Then the greeting: *Estimado* for a man, *Estimada* for a woman, followed by the title and last name and a colon. "Estimada señora Herrera:" If you do not know the name, "Estimados señores:" or "A quien corresponda:" (To whom it may concern:) both work.

The first sentence names the purpose. Spanish has several ready phrases. "Le escribo para solicitar el puesto de…" (I am writing to apply for the position of…). "Me dirijo a usted para…" (I am addressing you in order to…). "Por medio de la presente…" (By means of this letter…) is older and very formal, common in Mexico. The verb *solicitar* means to apply for or request; the noun *la solicitud* is an application. *El puesto* is a position or job opening.

The body gives two or three short paragraphs: who you are, what you offer, when you are available. Then the closing sentences, which are nearly fixed: "Adjunto mi currículum" (I attach my résumé). "Le agradezco de antemano su atención" (I thank you in advance for your attention). "Quedo a su disposición para cualquier pregunta" (I remain at your disposal for any question). The final line is one word or two: *Atentamente* (Sincerely), *Cordialmente* (Cordially), or "Un cordial saludo" (A cordial greeting), then a comma, then your full name.

Compare this with an English business letter and you will find the same bones: date, greeting, purpose, body, closing, name. What is different is the details: the colon, the lowercase month, Estimado instead of Dear, and the usted forms throughout. Get the bones right and the letter reads as serious. Get the details right and it reads as fluent.

words.d: Dear (formal) — Estimada señora Herrera: with a colon; use Estimados señores: if you do not know the name
Sincerely — the standard closing of a formal letter, followed by a comma and your name
to apply for, to request — Le escribo para solicitar el puesto; la solicitud is the application
the position, the job opening — el puesto de ayudante de cocina
to attach — Adjunto mi currículum (I attach my résumé)
the résumé — also el currículum vitae or el CV

look.title: The Letter, Piece by Piece
look.text: Chicago, 14 de abril de 2026. Estimada señora Herrera: Le escribo para solicitar el puesto de ayudante de cocina que anunció en su tienda. Soy estudiante de último año en Chicago, hablo inglés y español, y tengo experiencia sirviendo en eventos de mi parroquia. Estoy disponible de junio a agosto, de lunes a sábado. Adjunto mi currículum. Le agradezco de antemano su atención y quedo a su disposición. Atentamente, Andrés Maldonado.
look.prompt: Label the six parts: date, greeting, purpose, body, closing sentences, signature. Find every usted form and every possessive su.

check.q: Which greeting is correct for a formal letter to a woman whose name you know?
check.why: Estimada agrees with a woman, the title is lowercase, and the greeting ends in a colon. Querida is for friends and family; Estimado is masculine.

check.q: How is the date written at the top of a Spanish letter?
check.why: The pattern is city, day, de, month in lowercase, de, year. Months are not capitalized in Spanish.

check.q: "Le escribo para solicitar el puesto." What is the writer doing?
check.why: Solicitar el puesto means to apply for the position. Le escribo para introduces the letter's purpose.

lessons.title: Saying What You Offer
lessons.mainIdea: The body of an application uses short, confident sentences about experience, skills and availability, all in the usted register and without slang.
reading: Andrés's first draft said "soy buena onda y trabajo duro." *Buena onda* (cool, easygoing) is Mexican slang, warm and friendly, and exactly wrong for a stranger reading job applications. The second draft replaced it with facts: a grade level, two languages, a kind of *experiencia* (experience). Formal writing prefers what you have done and what you can do over how you would describe your personality.

Here are sentences that do that work. "Tengo experiencia en…" (I have experience in…): tengo experiencia en servicio al cliente, en cocina, en cuidado de niños. "Soy responsable y puntual" (I am responsible and punctual): adjectives about work habits are fine; adjectives like simpático or divertido are for friends. "Hablo inglés y español" is one of your strongest lines in Chicago. "Estoy disponible de junio a agosto, de lunes a sábado" (I am available from June to August, Monday to Saturday) tells the *empresa* (company) what it needs to schedule you.

Say why this job, in one sentence. "Me interesa el puesto porque quiero aprender el negocio de la comida" (I am interested in the position because I want to learn the food business). Then offer the next step: "Estoy disponible para una entrevista cuando usted lo considere conveniente" (I am available for an interview whenever you consider it convenient). *La entrevista* is the interview, and *conveniente* here means suitable, not the English sense of easy.

Keep every verb in the usted register and every sentence short. No exclamation points, no emoji, no "jaja." If you are a heritage speaker, this is where your school Spanish and your home Spanish meet: the vocabulary you grew up with, arranged with the care of an essay. Read it aloud once; if a line sounds like something you would text, rewrite it.

words.d: experience — Tengo experiencia en servicio al cliente (I have experience in customer service)
available — Estoy disponible de junio a agosto
punctual, on time — Soy responsable y puntual
the company, the business — su empresa (your company)
the interview — Estoy disponible para una entrevista

look.title: The Job Posting, in Numbers
rows: Salario por hora en dólares (hourly wage)
Semanas del programa (weeks of the program)
look.cite: Example job posting written for this lesson; figures are illustrative
look.prompt: Using these numbers, write one sentence in Spanish stating your availability that matches the posting. How many dollars would twenty hours at this wage earn in a week?

check.q: Which sentence belongs in a formal job application?
choices: Soy buena onda y me llevo bien con todos.
Tengo experiencia en servicio al cliente.
check.why: Tengo experiencia en… states a fact in a formal register. Buena onda, jaja, súper and avísame (a tú command) belong to informal speech.

check.q: "Estoy disponible de lunes a viernes" means
choices: I am busy Monday through Friday.
I am available Monday through Friday.
I am free only on Friday.
check.why: Disponible means available, and de lunes a viernes is from Monday to Friday.

check.q: Why does the second letter replace "me puedes llamar cuando quieras" with "estoy disponible para una entrevista cuando usted lo considere conveniente"?
choices: Because the first sentence has a grammar error
Because the first sentence is too long
Because the second uses usted and formal vocabulary for a stranger
Because cuando quieras is not Spanish
check.why: Both are correct Spanish. The second matches the register: usted, considere, conveniente. The first uses tú and a casual tone meant for a friend.

lessons.title: Informal Messages and Texting
lessons.mainIdea: Informal Spanish messages open with Hola or ¿Qué tal?, close with un abrazo or nos vemos, and in texts shorten words: q, xq, tqm, bn.
reading: Everything about formal letters has an informal twin, and you probably already use it. An informal message opens with "Hola, Luis" or "¿Qué tal?" (How's it going?). In Mexico you hear "¿Qué onda?"; in Argentina, "¿Cómo andás?"; in Spain, "¿Qué pasa?" The greeting can end with a comma or a colon, and the verbs are all tú (or vos). The closing is warm: *un abrazo* (a hug), *besos* (kisses, common among friends and family, especially women), *cuídate* (take care), *nos vemos* (see you).

Text messages shorten Spanish the way they shorten English. *Q* stands for que, *xq* or *pq* for porque, *tqm* for te quiero mucho, *bn* for bien, *mñn* for mañana, *tb* for también, *salu2* for saludos, and *jajaja* is how Spanish laughs (never hahaha, because Spanish h is silent and j makes the sound). Accents and inverted marks often disappear in texts, and "k" sometimes replaces "qu": "k haces" for qué haces. This is not bad Spanish; it is texting Spanish, and speakers switch out of it the moment they write anything else.

The line between registers is about the reader. A text to a cousin: "Oye, ¿vienes mñn? Trae la música. Un abrazo." (Hey, are you coming tomorrow? Bring the music. A hug.) An email to a teacher: "Estimada profesora Vega: Le escribo para preguntar si puedo entregar el ensayo el lunes. Le agradezco su comprensión. Atentamente, Andrés." Same student, same day, two registers. Andrés knew both; the story's problem was only that he used the first one for a stranger.

One warning for heritage speakers and everyone else. Texting habits leak. If you write xq and jajaja all day, they will try to sneak into an essay or a job application. Proofread specifically for them: every que spelled out, every accent in place, every ¿ and ¡ present. A single tqm in a cover letter undoes a whole page of good work.

words.d: the message — un mensaje de texto is a text message
How's it going? — an informal greeting used everywhere; also ¿Qué onda? in Mexico
a hug — a warm informal closing for a message or letter
take care — a tú command used as an informal goodbye; cuídese with usted
hahaha — Spanish laughter is spelled with j because h is silent

look.title: Decode the Text
look.text: Andrés gets this text from his cousin: "Oye q onda, xq no viniste ayer? Mñn hay partido a las 5, vienes? Tqm, salu2." Written out in full Spanish: Oye, ¿qué onda? ¿Por qué no viniste ayer? Mañana hay partido a las cinco, ¿vienes? Te quiero mucho, saludos. (Hey, what's up? Why didn't you come yesterday? Tomorrow there's a game at five, are you coming? Love you, cheers.)
look.prompt: Write the cousin's message as a formal note to a coach who wants to know why you missed practice. What changes besides the abbreviations?

check.q: In a Spanish text, xq stands for
check.why: The x stands for por (as in multiplication) and q for que, so xq reads as por qué or porque depending on the sentence.

check.q: Which closing belongs at the end of a message to a close friend?
check.why: Un abrazo is a warm, informal closing. The other three are fixed phrases of a formal letter.

check.q: Why does Spanish write laughter as jajaja and not hahaha?
choices: Because Spanish has no letter h
Because h is silent in Spanish and j makes the sound
Because jajaja is a word borrowed from English
check.why: Spanish h is always silent, so hahaha would make no sound. The letter j gives the breathy sound of laughter.

lessons.title: Softening a Request
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish makes a request more polite by moving from puede to podría, from quiero to quisiera, and by adding por favor and ¿sería posible…?
reading: At the bakery, Andrés could ask for an application form three ways. "Dame una solicitud" (give me an application) is a command; it is what you say to a brother. "¿Me da una solicitud?" (will you give me an application?) is neutral and polite with usted. "¿Me podría dar una solicitud, por favor?" (could you give me an application, please?) is soft and respectful. The verb moved from da to *podría*, and that one change is the heart of polite Spanish.

*Podría* is the conditional of poder, and the conditional is the register-softener. "¿Puede ayudarme?" (can you help me?) becomes "¿Podría ayudarme?" (could you help me?). *Quisiera* (I would like) is the polite form of quiero (I want): "Quisiera hablar con la señora Herrera." *Me gustaría* (I would like) works the same way. "¿Sería posible…?" (would it be possible…?) is the gentlest of all: "¿Sería posible empezar en junio?" English does the same trick with could and would; Spanish just has a clear ending for it.

Two more tools. *Por favor* can go at the start or the end. *Disculpe* (excuse me, usted form) opens a request to a stranger or an elder: "Disculpe, ¿sabe dónde está la oficina?" With a friend you say *disculpa* or *perdona*. And the phrase "¿Me haría el favor de…?" (would you do me the favor of…) is very polite and common in Mexico and Central America: "¿Me haría el favor de firmar aquí?"

When you thank someone formally, "muchas gracias" is always right, and "le agradezco" (I thank you) or "se lo agradezco mucho" (I am very grateful to you for it) raises the register. Reply to thanks with "de nada" or, more formally, "no hay de qué" or "a sus órdenes" (at your service), which you will hear from shopkeepers and waiters throughout Mexico.

words.d: could you, could I — the conditional of poder, the polite form of puede: ¿Podría ayudarme?
I would like — the polite form of quiero: Quisiera hablar con la dueña
excuse me (usted) — to get a stranger's attention; disculpa with tú
Would it be possible…? — the gentlest way to ask: ¿Sería posible empezar en junio?
the favor — por favor (please); ¿Me haría el favor de…? (Would you do me the favor of…?)

look.title: Three Ways to Ask for the Same Thing
look.text: To a little brother: Pásame el pan. (Pass me the bread.) To a classmate: ¿Me pasas el pan, por favor? To an elder at the table: ¿Me podría pasar el pan, por favor? Now at the bakery: To a friend behind the counter: Dame una solicitud. To a clerk you do not know: ¿Me da una solicitud, por favor? To the owner: Disculpe, señora, ¿sería posible obtener una solicitud?
look.prompt: For each set, what exactly changes from the first line to the third? Say the most polite version aloud with the tone you would really use.

check.q: Which request is the most polite?
choices: ¿Me podría dar el formulario, por favor?
check.why: Podría (conditional) plus por favor is the softest form. Dame is a command, me das is casual, and quiero states a want.

check.q: "Quisiera" is the polite form of
check.why: Quisiera softens quiero (I want) into I would like. Quería is the imperfect, querré the future, quise the preterite.

check.q: To get the attention of a stranger you address as usted, you say
check.why: Disculpe is the usted form. Disculpa and perdona are tú forms; oye is an informal hey.

lessons.title: Elders, Teachers and Employers
lessons.mainIdea: With elders, teachers and employers, usted plus a title, a greeting by time of day, and small courtesies like con permiso and mande show respect.
reading: In many Spanish-speaking families, register begins at home. Grandparents and older relatives are often addressed as usted: "Abuela, ¿cómo está?" "Tío, ¿usted quiere café?" Not every family does this; in Spain most grandchildren say tú, and in Argentina vos. But in many Mexican, Central American, Colombian and Caribbean families, using usted with elders is a sign of how you were raised, and slipping into tú can earn a look. If you are a heritage speaker, you already know your family's rule. If you are not, follow what you hear.

Teachers are usted, with a title: "Buenos días, maestra Ruiz," "profesor Vega, ¿tiene un minuto?" The short *profe* is affectionate and common among students, but it is for the hallway, not a letter. Employers are usted and señor or señora until they say otherwise. Greetings by time of day matter more in Spanish than in English: *buenos días* until midday, *buenas tardes* until evening, *buenas noches* after dark, and it is normal to greet everyone in a room when you enter and to say goodbye when you leave.

Some small phrases carry a great deal. *Con permiso* (with your permission) is what you say when you pass in front of someone, leave a table, or enter a room. *Mande* is how many Mexicans answer when an elder or a customer calls them; it means something like yes? or at your service, and it is far more respectful than ¿qué? In Mexico a shopkeeper or waiter may say "a sus órdenes" (at your orders) or "para servirle" (at your service) after helping you; the polite reply is gracias.

Body language is register too. A handshake with an adult you meet for the first time; a kiss on one cheek (two in Spain) between friends and family; standing when an elder enters; not interrupting. None of these is a grammar rule, and all of them are part of speaking Spanish well. Andrés knew every one of them from his grandmother's kitchen. The job letter just asked him to bring them onto the page.

words.d: excuse me, with your permission — said when passing in front of someone or leaving a room
yes? at your service — a respectful reply in Mexico when someone calls you; more polite than ¿qué?
good morning — until midday; then buenas tardes and, after dark, buenas noches
teacher (affectionate short form of profesor, profesora) — for speech, not for letters
at your service — a courteous phrase from shopkeepers and waiters in Mexico

look.title: Sunday at Abuela's
look.text: Andrés arrives at his grandmother's apartment in Back of the Yards. Abuela: ¡Andrés! Andrés: Mande, abuela. Buenas tardes. ¿Cómo está? Abuela: Bien, mijo. Pasa, pasa. ¿Ya comiste? Andrés: Todavía no. Con permiso. (He passes in front of his great-uncle to sit down.) Tío Manuel, ¿usted quiere más café? Tío: No, gracias, hijo. His grandmother says tú to him; he says usted to her and to his great-uncle. That is the rule in this family.
look.prompt: Find three signs of respect in Andrés's lines. Which of them would you also use with a teacher, and which are only for family?

check.q: "Mande" is used in Mexico to
choices: answer respectfully when someone calls your name
check.why: Mande is a respectful reply, roughly yes? or at your service, when an elder or customer calls you. It is preferred over ¿qué? in Mexico.

check.q: You need to walk in front of your friend's grandmother to reach a chair. You say
check.why: Con permiso asks permission to pass or to leave. Mande answers a call, a sus órdenes offers service, and buenas noches is a greeting.

check.q: Which greeting fits a teacher at 8:00 in the morning?
check.why: Buenos días is the morning greeting, and maestra plus the last name is the respectful form. Qué onda is slang; buenas tardes and buenas noches are for later in the day.

lessons.title: False Friends
lessons.mainIdea: False friends look like English words but mean something else: embarazada is pregnant, éxito is success, carpeta is a folder.
reading: A *falso amigo* (false friend) is a Spanish word that looks like an English word and means something different. They are dangerous in exactly the situations this chapter is about, because a false friend in a job letter or a conversation with an employer can change your meaning completely. The most famous is *embarazada*. It means pregnant, not embarrassed. "Estoy embarazada" is an announcement, not an apology. Embarrassed is *avergonzado* or *avergonzada*, or "me da vergüenza."

*Éxito* means success, not exit. "Le deseo mucho éxito" (I wish you much success) is a lovely closing line. The way out is *la salida*. *Carpeta* is a folder or binder, not a carpet; the carpet is *la alfombra*, an Arabic word you met last chapter. *Librería* is a bookstore; a library is *la biblioteca*. *Ropa* is clothing, not rope. *Sopa* is soup, not soap (*jabón*). *Largo* means long, not large (*grande*).

Verbs and adverbs have false friends too. *Asistir* means to attend, not to assist: "Asistí a la reunión" is I attended the meeting; to help is ayudar. *Actualmente* means currently, not actually: "Actualmente estudio en Chicago." Actually is *en realidad*. *Realizar* means to carry out or accomplish, not to realize: "Realicé un proyecto." To realize is *darse cuenta*. *Sensible* means sensitive, not sensible; sensible is *sensato*. And *molestar* means to bother or annoy, nothing more: "Perdón por molestarlo" is Sorry to bother you.

The fix is to notice the pattern: when a Spanish word looks exactly like English, check it. Many look-alikes are true friends (hospital, familia, importante, universidad). The false ones are a short list, and once you know them they stop being traps. Write "Le deseo mucho éxito" at the end of a note to a teacher and you will sound exactly right.

words.d: pregnant — not embarrassed, which is avergonzado/a or me da vergüenza
success — not exit, which is la salida; Le deseo mucho éxito
the folder, binder — not carpet, which is la alfombra
the bookstore — not library, which is la biblioteca
currently, nowadays — not actually, which is en realidad
to attend — Asistí a la reunión; to assist or help is ayudar

look.title: Catch the False Friend
look.text: Andrés's classmate Kevin writes to his teacher: "Estimada profesora: Estoy muy embarazado porque no asistí a clase ayer. Actualmente, tenía una cita con el doctor. Dejé mi carpeta en la librería. Le deseo mucho éxito. Atentamente, Kevin." The teacher understands but smiles: embarazado is the wrong word (Kevin means avergonzado), actualmente should be en realidad (actually), and librería is fine if he means the bookstore, but he meant the library, la biblioteca. The last line, though, is perfect.
look.prompt: Rewrite Kevin's note with the three false friends corrected. Which sentence had the right word all along?

check.q: "Mi hermana está embarazada" means
check.why: Embarazada means pregnant. Embarrassed is avergonzada or me da vergüenza.

check.q: Which sentence uses éxito correctly?
choices: El éxito está a la derecha del edificio.
Le deseo mucho éxito en su nuevo trabajo.
check.why: Éxito means success, so wishing someone mucho éxito is correct. The other sentences need la salida (exit).

check.q: "Actualmente vivo en Cicero." The best English translation is
choices: I used to live in Cicero.
check.why: Actualmente means currently or nowadays, not actually. Actually would be en realidad.

lessons.title: Signs on the Street
lessons.mainIdea: Public signs use short formal Spanish: usted commands, the impersonal se (se vende, se prohíbe), and a few fixed words like salida, empuje and tire.
reading: Walk down 26th Street in Little Village and you can read a whole lesson in register on the storefronts. *Abierto* (open) and *cerrado* (closed). *Entrada* (entrance) and *salida* (exit, not éxito). *Empuje* (push) and *tire* (pull) on doors; in Mexico and much of Latin America pull is often *jale*. *Baños* or *servicios* (restrooms). *Caja* (cash register, checkout). *Rebajas* or *ofertas* (sales, deals). These are the most formal register of all: no pronoun, no greeting, just the word.

Signs that tell you what to do use the usted command or the infinitive: "Empuje" (push), "No fumar" (no smoking), "No estacionar" (no parking), "Favor de no tocar" (please do not touch, common in Mexico). Signs that state a rule use the impersonal *se*, which you met with reflexive verbs: "Se prohíbe fumar" (smoking is prohibited), "Se habla español" (Spanish is spoken here), "Se vende" (for sale), "Se alquila" or, in Mexico, "Se renta" (for rent), "Se busca" (wanted, as on a help-wanted sign: "Se busca ayudante").

*Prohibido* on its own is common and strong: "Prohibido el paso" (no entry), "Prohibido estacionarse" (no parking). Warnings use *cuidado* (careful) or *peligro* (danger): "Cuidado con el perro" (beware of the dog), "Peligro: alto voltaje" (danger: high voltage), "Piso mojado" (wet floor). And the sign that started Andrés's story: "Se solicita ayudante de cocina. Informes adentro." (Kitchen assistant wanted. Inquire inside.)

Reading signs is the fastest way to build formal vocabulary, because every word on a sign was chosen to be understood by everyone. Next time you are in Pilsen, La Villita or Humboldt Park, read every sign you pass and sort them: which ones give a command, which ones state a rule with se, and which ones simply name the place.

words.d: the exit — la salida de emergencia; the opposite is la entrada
push, pull — usted commands on doors; in Mexico, pull is often jale
prohibited, forbidden — Prohibido el paso (no entry); Se prohíbe fumar
for sale — the impersonal se; also se alquila or se renta (for rent), se busca (wanted)
the sales, markdowns — a sign in a shop window; also ofertas

look.title: Ten Signs on One Block
look.text: Read these signs from a walk down 18th Street and say what each means: 1. Abierto. 2. Empuje. 3. Se habla español. 4. Rebajas de verano. 5. No estacionar. 6. Se renta departamento. 7. Cuidado con el perro. 8. Baños solo para clientes. 9. Salida de emergencia. 10. Se solicita cajera. Sort them: which are simple labels, which are commands, and which use se to state a rule or an offer?
look.prompt: Which sign would you look for if you were leaving in a hurry? Which one is a job opening, and what is the job?

check.q: A door in Mexico City says JALE. You should
check.why: Jale is the Mexican word for pull on a door; Spain and many other places use tire. Empuje means push.

check.q: "Se busca mesero" on a restaurant window means
choices: The waiter is looking for you.
check.why: Se busca with a job title is a help-wanted sign: a waiter is being sought. The impersonal se has no specific subject.

check.q: Which sign tells you the way out?
check.why: Salida is the exit. Éxito is a false friend meaning success, entrada is the entrance, and caja is the checkout.

lessons.title: Reading a Menu and Ordering
lessons.mainIdea: A Spanish menu is organized into entradas, platos principales, postres and bebidas, and ordering politely uses quisiera, me trae and ¿me podría traer la cuenta?
reading: Back at the restaurant in Pilsen, the three friends from the last chapter read a menu that any Spanish speaker can navigate. It is divided into *entradas* (appetizers; also aperitivos or, in Mexico, antojitos for small snacks), *platos principales* or *platos fuertes* (main dishes), *postres* (desserts) and *bebidas* (drinks). A *menú del día* (daily menu) or *comida corrida* in Mexico is a fixed-price meal of two or three courses, usually the cheapest way to eat well at lunchtime.

Ordering is register in action. The waiter, using usted, asks "¿Qué desea?" or "¿Qué le traigo?" (What would you like? What can I bring you?). You answer with the polite forms you learned: "Quisiera los tacos al pastor, por favor," "Para mí, el pollo," or "¿Me trae un agua de horchata?" Asking for the check: "La cuenta, por favor" is fine; "¿Me podría traer la cuenta?" is softer. Two things to look for in small print: *propina incluida* (tip included) and *IVA incluido* (sales tax included). In much of Latin America and Spain the tax is already in the price, and tipping customs vary; in the United States, tip as you normally would.

Spanish menus often carry the vocabulary of the last chapter. A Mexican menu lists elotes, frijoles and aguacate; an Argentine one lists choclo, porotos and palta; a Puerto Rican one lists habichuelas and, for fried plantains, tostones. A Spanish menu lists patatas and zumo. Reading a menu from another country is a small test of everything you know about regional words, and context, as always, helps: a word under postres is a dessert whether or not you have seen it before.

One more courtesy: when you finish and others are still eating, or when you pass a table where people are eating, Spanish speakers say *buen provecho* (enjoy your meal). It is expected in Mexico and Central America, common in Spain, and a small sign that you know how to be at a table.

words.d: the appetizer — on a menu; also the entrance on a sign
the main dish — also el plato fuerte in Mexico
the dessert — flan, arroz con leche and tres leches are common postres
the check, the bill — La cuenta, por favor; ¿Me podría traer la cuenta?
the tip — propina incluida means the tip is already on the bill
the daily fixed-price meal — comida corrida in Mexico

look.title: Menú del Día, Example Prices
rows: Menú del día: sopa, plato principal, postre y bebida
look.cite: Example menu written for this lesson; prices are illustrative
look.prompt: If you order the soup, the tacos, the flan and the horchata separately, what is the total? How much do you save with the menú del día? Order it in Spanish, politely.

check.q: Under which heading would you find flan?
check.why: Flan is a dessert, so it appears under postres. Entradas are appetizers, bebidas drinks, platos fuertes main dishes.

check.q: Which is the most polite way to ask for the check?
choices: ¿Me podría traer la cuenta, por favor?
check.why: Podría plus por favor is the polite register with a waiter you address as usted. Dame is a tú command; the others are abrupt.

check.q: "Propina incluida" at the bottom of a bill means
check.why: Propina is the tip; incluida means included. The line tells you the service charge is already on the bill.

lessons.title: Reading News Headlines
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish headlines drop articles, use the present tense for past events, and pack a whole story into a few formal words.
reading: The last authentic text is the hardest to read and the most useful: the *titular* (headline) of a *periódico* (newspaper). Spanish-language papers are everywhere: El País in Madrid, Clarín in Buenos Aires, El Universal in Mexico City, El Nuevo Día in San Juan, and in Chicago the weekly La Raza and Spanish sections of larger outlets. Their headlines follow rules that make them look strange until you know the pattern.

First, headlines drop articles. "Gobierno anuncia nuevo plan de transporte" reads Government announces new transportation plan; in a full sentence it would be El gobierno anuncia un nuevo plan de transporte. Second, they use the present tense for things that already happened, to sound immediate: "Lluvias dejan tres heridos en el sur" (Rains leave three injured in the south) describes yesterday's storm. Third, they use short formal verbs you rarely say aloud: *anunciar* (to announce), *aprobar* (to approve), *rechazar* (to reject), *dejar* with a number (to leave, as in leave injured), *subir* and *bajar* (to rise, to fall) for prices and temperatures.

Fourth, headlines love numbers and place names. "Sube 8% el precio de la gasolina" (Gas price rises 8%). "Chicago celebra el Desfile de la Independencia Mexicana en La Villita" (Chicago celebrates the Mexican Independence Parade in Little Village). Once you know these four rules, a headline becomes a sentence with the small words removed. Put them back and read it aloud: subject, verb, what, where.

Everything in a newspaper is formal register. News articles use usted in interviews, full names with titles, and no slang. Reading one headline a day, in a paper from a country you are curious about, is one of the best habits a Spanish student can have. You will learn the vocabulary of the *noticia* (news story), and you will see how the same language handles Buenos Aires, Madrid, Mexico City and Chicago in one style.

words.d: the headline — titulares drop articles and use the present tense for past events
the newspaper — also el diario; El Universal is a periódico of Mexico City
the news story, a piece of news — las noticias is the news in general
to announce — Gobierno anuncia nuevo plan (Government announces new plan)
the government — often the subject of a headline, without its article

look.title: Unpack the Headline
look.text: Headline: Alcaldía aprueba nuevo parque en Pilsen; vecinos celebran. (City government approves new park in Pilsen; neighbors celebrate.) As full sentences: La alcaldía aprobó un nuevo parque en Pilsen. Los vecinos celebraron. What changed: two articles returned (la, un, los), and the present tense (aprueba, celebran) became the preterite (aprobó, celebraron), because the event already happened. Now try this one on your own: Baja la temperatura y cierran escuelas en el norte de Illinois.
look.prompt: Rewrite the second headline as two full sentences with articles and past-tense verbs. Which word tells you it is about weather?

check.q: "Gobierno anuncia nuevo plan" as a full sentence would be
choices: El gobierno anuncia un nuevo plan.
El gobierno anuncias un nuevo plan.
Un gobierno anuncia el nuevo plan.
check.why: Headlines drop articles; the full sentence restores el and un. Anuncias is the tú form and does not match gobierno.

check.q: Why do Spanish headlines use the present tense for events that already happened?
choices: Because Spanish has no past tense for news
To make the news sound immediate
Because the events are still happening
check.why: The present tense is a headline convention that makes the story feel current. The article itself uses the preterite.

check.q: "Sube el precio del pan" means
choices: The price of bread stays the same.
check.why: Subir means to rise or go up; bajar would mean to fall. Headlines use subir and bajar for prices and temperatures.

review.q: Which sentence correctly addresses the owner of a company you have never met?
review.why: Usted takes the él/ella form puede. Puedes is tú, podés is vos, and podéis is vosotros; all three are informal.

review.q: Which title goes with a first name?
review.why: Don and doña take a first name: don Manuel, doña Carmen. The others take a last name.

review.q: The correct closing of a formal letter is
review.why: Atentamente (Sincerely) closes a formal letter. Besos, un abrazo and nos vemos are informal closings for friends and family.

review.q: "¿Podría decirme dónde está la salida?" is polite because
choices: it uses the conditional podría and the usted form
it uses tú and por favor
review.why: Podría is the conditional of poder, the softener of polite Spanish, and decirme keeps the usted register. Salida, not éxito, is the exit.

review.q: Which word is a false friend?
review.why: Carpeta looks like carpet but means folder. Hospital, familia and importante mean what they look like.

review.q: A sign reads "Se prohíbe fumar." It means
review.why: Se prohíbe is the impersonal se with prohibir: smoking is prohibited. The sign states a rule with no specific subject.
Tqm is the texting abbreviation for te quiero mucho (I love you a lot). Tb is también.

review.q: The headline "Vecinos celebran nuevo mercado en Humboldt Park" as a full past-tense sentence is
choices: Los vecinos celebraron un nuevo mercado en Humboldt Park.
Vecinos celebraron nuevo mercado en Humboldt Park.
Los vecinos celebran el nuevo mercado en Humboldt Park.
Los vecinos celebrarán un nuevo mercado en Humboldt Park.
review.why: Restore the articles (los, un) and change the headline present to the preterite (celebraron). Celebrarán is the future.
